newsitem.title: THAILAND: Australia's Downer seeks to calm racism fears.
newsitem.headline: Australia's Downer seeks to calm racism fears.

text.p: Australian Foreign Minister Alexander Downer said in a Thai newspaper on Monday that his government was unequivocally committed to an immigration policy that would not discriminate against Asians.
In an article published on the front page of The Nation newspaper, Downer wrote that Asian nations should see through racist sentiments stirred by a small minority of Australians.
Remarks made by independent Australian member of parliament Pauline Hanson last month sparked a heated debate on racism and immigation in Australia.

Hanson, dumped from Prime Minister John Howard's Liberal Party this year for controversial comments about Australian aboriginals, complained in her maiden parliamentary speech that Australia was being swamped by Asians and called for a halt to immigration.

"Each year around 40 percent of immigrants to Australia come from Asia, helping to create a successful multi-ethnic society," Downer wrote. "The Australian government is unequivocally committed to maintaining a non-discriminatory immigration policy."

He said a small minority may occassionally "stir up a ruckus", amplified by the media that rightly sees intolerance as a challenge to Australia's fundamental values. But most Australians believed in a "fair-go" for everyone in their country, regardless of race or background, the minister wrote.
"Our friends in the region need to see us through the hype and recognise that Australian is going forward, not backwards," he said.
Australia understood that much of its future lay in a closer partnership with its Asian neighbours, Downer maintained.
"Immigration is one of the most important strands of the web of ties we are building with Asian countries. The Australian government will ensure that stays the case," Downer said.

He also cited the case of two Asians - China-born pediatrican John Yu who was voted Australian of the Year in 1996 and Cambodian Hong Lim who was elected to the Victorian state parliament - as individuals who had helped make Australia a vibrant, open and tolerant society.
But the foreign minister stressed Hanson had a right to say what she said because Australia was an open society and people were free to air their views.
He also defended prime minister Howard's handling of the racism debate so far. Howard has been criticised recently by some Asian newspapers for failing to repudiate Hanson's comments.
The Australian government and opposition joined in a bipartisan resolution in parliament last week condemning racism and pledging tolerance.
The Bangkok Post newspaper said on Monday in a commentary that it was a great irony that Hanson was not present in parliament when the resolution was passed.

The paper's editor Pichai Chuensuksawadi said in the commentary entitled "Asians will be watching Australia", that Hanson had now called for a national referendum on immigration and appeared determined to pursue the anti-Asian debate.
"How the Australian government, opposition and people handle this debate from here on remains to be seen. What is certain is that Asian eyes will be watching," he warned.
